lessons.title: Managing structural fumigations at work
lessons.html:
The full process in the workplace

In this module you take part in complete structural fumigations, from planning to hand-back, under a registered fumigator. Jobs may include tarping a house for drywood termites or borers, sealing a flour mill or food factory for stored product insects, fumigating containers of wood packaging for export, or treating furniture under sheets. You will see how management decisions are made and practise taking more responsibility as your competence grows.

Stages you will take part in

  1. Pre-fumigation inspection and volume measurement.
  2. Writing or reviewing the fumigation management plan and risk assessment.
  3. Notifying occupants, neighbours and others as required.
  4. Preparation: evacuation, removal of items the label requires, sealing or tarping, signage, lockout and the occupancy check.
  5. Dose calculation, checked by a second person, and introduction of fumigant.
  6. Monitoring concentration and perimeter during exposure.
  7. Aeration, clearance testing and the clearance certificate.
  8. Residue handling, equipment care and the client hand-back.

Scenario: a family home with borers

A family home has active wood borer damage in the roof timbers throughout. The plan calls for a tarp fumigation. During preparation the family's elderly neighbour, whose house is two metres away, says she cannot leave. Your supervisor visits her with you, explains the risk, increases perimeter monitoring at her windows, and agrees with her family that she stays with relatives for the exposure and aeration. The job proceeds only when she has left. Managing people is as important as managing gas.

lessons.title: Management responsibilities and evidence
lessons.html:
What managing a fumigation involves

Beyond the technical steps, the person managing a structural fumigation is responsible for decisions, people and records.

ResponsibilityExamples
Legal complianceRegistered operator in charge, registered product used as labelled, records kept
PeopleTeam competence and roles, occupants, neighbours, public
Go or no-go decisionsWeather, sealing quality, occupancy, equipment readiness
IncidentsLeaks, exposures, unauthorised entry, damage
Client relationshipClear communication, certificate, follow-up

Go or no-go

Practise the decision with your mentor before each introduction: Is the structure sealed? Are all people and animals out, confirmed by two people? Are signs, guards and monitors in place? Is the weather suitable? Is the dose checked? If any answer is no, the fumigation does not start.

Learning from each job

After each fumigation, hold a short debrief: what went well, what nearly went wrong, and what should change. Record lessons in your logbook.

Portfolio evidence

  • Fumigation management plans you helped prepare.
  • Volume and dose calculations with checks.
  • Completed logs, clearance records and certificates you were part of.
  • Debrief notes and mentor sign-offs.

Key points

  • Take part in every stage from inspection to hand-back under a registered fumigator.
  • Managing people, including neighbours, is as important as managing gas.
  • Use a strict go or no-go check before fumigant is introduced.
  • The manager is responsible for compliance, people, decisions, incidents and records.
  • Debrief after each job and record lessons and sign-offs.
